newsitem.title: CANADA: Wildcat strikes hit British Columbia lumber talks.
newsitem.headline: Wildcat strikes hit British Columbia lumber talks.

text.p: British Columbia's coastal forest companies cancelled contract talks with the lumber workers' union on Friday after wildcat strikes at International Forest Products Ltd, a union official said.

Interfor was hit by wildcat strikes Friday at virtually all its operations in the lower mainland of British Columbia after giving layoff notices to workers at its McDonald cedar mill, said Sonny Ghag, president of the IWA-Canada local union for the Fraser Valley.
Forest Industrial Relations, which bargains on behalf of 65 forestry companies, pulled out of talks set for Friday morning after the job action.
"They are refusing to meet with us," said Ghag.
Forest Industrial Relations officials were not immediately available for comment.
Jack Draper, a general manager at Interfor, said the company was still trying to confirm the extent of job action at its operations but he said six to seven of its plants were closed.
"They are not operating," he said, referring to Interfor's sawmills and one remanufacturing plant.
The strikes followed an announcement by the company of plans to close the McDonald sawmill, which employs 135 workers, in October because of a shortage of logs.

The company will replace the sawmill with a wood remanufacturing plant on the same site which will employ 40 workers starting early next year. Interfor is offering other jobs to a futher 49 workers, Draper said. "But there will be some reduction in the work force," he said.
IWA-Canada union president Dave Haggard expressed anger at the break-off in contract talks and said it seemed unlikely they would resume until the strikes were over.
"It would appear they are frozen until that ends. FIR made it very clear they won't meet while the strike is on," he said.
While the two sides were divided over the issue of wages, Haggard said a contract deal might have been reached within a week if negotiations had continued.

He blamed Interfor for announcing the mill closure at the tail end of negotiations and said the company should have known it would agitate workers. The wildcat strikes did not have backing from the union leadership.
